advisor_letter:
Dear [[CLIENT_NAME]] and [[SPOUSE_NAME]],

Thank you for trusting BuildFi with a question that rarely sits still in anyone's mind: will the life you are building hold together once the paycheques stop? You are still in your accumulating years, and that matters more than it might feel right now, because the decisions you make in this stretch tend to compound the most. With children heading toward university and an aging parent who may lean on you, your plan is being asked to carry more than one generation at once.

You have already done real work to get here. As a couple, you have assembled a registered and non-registered base in the mid-six-figures, with public pensions forming a meaningful backbone of your future income. Choosing to plan together, rather than as two separate sets of numbers, is a structural decision that shapes everything that follows.

This report is built to be read in pieces. The executive summary gives you the verdict in thirty seconds. Chapter I lays out the foundations and the projection of where your wealth could travel. Chapter II describes the risk you would be taking under less forgiving markets. Chapter III walks through strategies and the decisions in front of you, and Chapter IV offers alternatives you could test. I encourage particular attention to Chapter II, because the spread between calm and difficult futures is where this plan would be defined.

Read it at your own pace, and treat every line as an observation rather than an instruction. Warmly, your BuildFi analysis team. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.
overall_assessment: Your plan currently carries a success rate of **44%**, a grade that signals real strain rather than collapse — meaningful margin exists but the trajectory would benefit from adjustments. The clearest strength is your public-pension backbone, with guaranteed income coverage near **54%** giving you a floor that does not depend on markets. The central risk is durability: in a median outcome, savings could be exhausted well before the end of the horizon, leaving the later years reliant on government income alone. The single lever that appears to move this picture the most is the gap between spending and sustainable withdrawals, and a certified financial planner could help map how far it would need to shift.
verdict: A **44%** success rate places this plan in fragile territory, where calm and difficult futures diverge sharply. The median and cautious scenarios both land at **0$** of real wealth at the horizon, while a favourable path preserves roughly **271K$** — a spread that shows the outcome hinges heavily on the order and strength of market returns. In plain terms, the plan could hold in good conditions but would struggle to absorb a poor sequence early in retirement.
page_zero_verdict: What seems to weigh on you most is whether two people, supporting both children and a parent, can retire without the whole structure tipping over. That is a fair thing to sit with, and this report is meant to make the path ahead clearer rather than heavier.
profile_summary: As a couple you hold roughly **368K$** in combined savings, split across registered, tax-free, and non-registered accounts — a diversification that gives you several levers rather than one. Your allocation sits at **60.3%** equity and **39.7%** bonds, a balanced posture that neither chases growth aggressively nor leaves you fully sheltered. The account mix is healthy; the question the projection raises is one of scale rather than structure.
trajectory_insight: The wealth trajectory shows a wide fan: a favourable path preserves about **271K$** in real terms, while both the median and cautious scenarios reach **0$** before the horizon closes. This means the projected wealth line crosses zero in the typical case, with the spread driven largely by how early and how harshly market returns disappoint. Whether the plan endures would depend heavily on the first decade after you stop working.
income_insight: Guaranteed income coverage sits at **54%**, meaning public benefits — led by QPP/CPP, with OAS alongside — form the backbone of your retirement income, and personal savings would add as a complement. Against monthly spending of **$7,200**, the projection shows a monthly gap of **$6,138** that withdrawals and other sources would need to bridge. That gap is the pressure point the rest of the plan responds to.
taxInsight: Across the full horizon, your projected lifetime tax in real terms is about **352K$**, against an average effective rate of **16.1%** — a moderate burden that reflects income drawn largely from pensions and modest withdrawals rather than large taxable gains. The projection records **0** years of OAS clawback, so high-income recovery of benefits does not appear to be a factor in your case. The dominant lever that emerges is the order in which accounts are drawn down, since coordinating registered and non-registered withdrawals can shift the tax savings detected year to year. As Ontario residents, your bracket exposure is somewhat gentler than it would be under Quebec's combined rates, which slightly eases the cost of each withdrawal. A certified financial planner could help structure that drawdown sequence.
estateInsight: The projection shows a net estate of **0$** with tax at death of **0$**, which reflects savings being fully drawn down within the horizon rather than any planning gap. Because no assets remain at the end of the typical scenario, estate transfer and deemed-disposition tax do not arise here. The focus for this profile sits earlier, on sustaining income through life rather than on what would pass afterward.
gis_insight: Once personal savings thin out, the projection indicates eligibility for the Guaranteed Income Supplement across roughly 13 years, contributing about 94K$ over your lifetime and around $7,267 per year on average. GIS is income-tested, and benefits are reduced by roughly 50¢ for each additional dollar of certain income, so the timing of withdrawals near those thresholds could matter. It functions as a backstop within the public-benefit floor rather than a destination to aim for.
riskInsight: The dispersion between the cautious scenario at **0$** and the favourable scenario at **271K$** is the defining feature of this plan's risk, and it points to sequence-of-returns — the order in which good and poor years arrive — as the dominant driver of the spread. Savings durability reflects this: in the projection, the portfolio could be depleted around age 74 if spending is not adjusted. Of the factors tested, an inflation increase weighs most heavily on the downside.
goals_insight: Your goal of "Children university tuition" at 80K$ shows a probability_met of **95%**, and "Aging parent care contribution" at 30K$ likewise sits at **95%**, both flagged on-track because they fall within years when median available assets remain ample. The strain in the plan appears later, in sustaining ongoing retirement income, rather than in funding these near-term family commitments.
stress_interpretation: Under stress, the plan is most vulnerable to stagflation, where success falls to 14% — a drop of roughly thirty points from the baseline — while a 2008-style shock at 25% is the scenario it weathers comparatively best. The pattern, with every scenario landing between 14% and 31%, indicates a plan whose endurance is tightly tied to inflation and the early sequence of returns rather than to any single isolated event. If a recovery path were to be tested, it could be sequenced as follows: first, stabilize the spending-to-withdrawal gap so the floor holds; then, adjust the drawdown order to stretch registered assets; and finally, re-plan the retirement-age and savings assumptions once the early years are steadier. A certified financial planner could help structure that sequence.
